analysis.one_liner: Repeals a list of long-standing tax breaks for oil and gas companies.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 17 House Democrats, was sent to the tax-writing committee in March 2023 and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end a series of special tax rules that lower what oil and gas companies pay in federal taxes. It would stretch out how quickly companies can deduct exploration costs, repeal credits for marginal wells and enhanced oil recovery, end deductions for drilling costs and a depreciation method called percentage depletion, bar the largest integrated oil companies from using a favorable inventory accounting method, tighten foreign tax credits, and make tar sands and oil shale fuels subject to petroleum excise taxes that fund oil spill cleanups.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit because the tax breaks the bill repeals shift costs that other taxpayers must make up. Drivers and communities near tar sands and oil shale transport also gain, since the bill makes those fuels pay into the petroleum excise tax that funds oil spill liability and cleanup.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and communities near oil transport

how_it_helps.text: Repeals tax credits for producing oil and gas from marginal wells and for enhanced oil recovery, and ends deductions for intangible drilling costs and tertiary injectants, so oil producers pay ordinary tax rates on those costs.
Repeals percentage depletion, a deduction that lets oil and gas producers write off a fixed percentage of gross income regardless of actual costs.
Prohibits major integrated oil companies from using last-in, first-out (LIFO) accounting, which lowers reported income and tax bills when prices rise.
Expands the definition of crude oil for excise tax purposes to include tar sands and oil shale-derived oil, so those fuels help fund the trust funds that pay for oil spill response and cleanup.
Limits the foreign tax credit for dual capacity taxpayers, closing a route by which oil companies reduce U.S. tax on income from countries that give them special economic benefits.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, and particularly the largest integrated producers, bear the cost of paying taxes they currently avoid through these provisions. Consumers could see some of the added cost passed through in fuel prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers, especially major integrated firms

drawbacks.text: Some of the repealed provisions, such as the marginal well credit and enhanced oil recovery credit, primarily benefit small and mid-sized producers of older wells; their removal could accelerate abandonment of stripper wells and modestly reduce domestic production.
Repealing tax preferences raises production costs, and fuel is a pass-through market, so some of the added cost would likely reach consumers at the pump.
The bill includes no provisions directing the new revenue to any specific public purpose; its benefits to ordinary people depend entirely on the general Treasury effect of higher tax collections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: ending special deductions and credits raises the cost of producing oil and gas, and a portion of that lands in fuel prices, especially for older marginal wells. Against that, these are industry-specific tax preferences that other businesses do not receive, the largest companies benefit most from the accounting rules, and tar sands-derived fuel currently escapes the excise tax that funds oil spill cleanups. The design is a clean repeal rather than a rebalancing, which keeps the pass-through to consumers as the main honest objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, joined by Reps. Casten and Porter as original cosponsors.
Seventeen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action afterward.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill advancing past its committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers keep the tax deductions, credits, and accounting methods the bill would have repealed, and taxpayers continue to absorb those costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies that kept their tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.role: Sponsor, member of the Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which stayed in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Major beneficiaries of the tax provisions the bill repeals
against.what_they_did: Opposed repeal of oil and gas tax subsidies and lobbied against such proposals.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill sat in committee under a Republican chair, so the fight ran along party lines, though no vote was ever taken to record the split.

industries.note: The bill repeals a package of deductions, credits, and accounting methods that lower their tax bills, raising their effective tax rate. Fuel is a pass-through market, so some of the added cost would reach consumers at the pump.
The LIFO accounting ban and the foreign tax credit limits target the largest integrated producers specifically, ending accounting treatment that reduces their tax on income when prices rise.
The marginal well credit and enhanced oil recovery credit they rely on would be repealed, making older wells costlier to operate and risking earlier abandonment.

industries.industry: Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund / pipeline and tanker transport of tar sands oil
industries.note: Tar sands and oil shale-derived fuels would newly pay the petroleum excise tax that finances oil spill cleanup, closing an exemption that let some shipments escape the fee while still posing spill risks.
